title: How to Verify Compliance AI Accuracy Before You Buy: An MGA Evaluation Guide (2026)
summary: How MGAs test compliance AI before buying: measure missed violations, not accuracy, and size the pilot by violations rather than policies.
body_markdown:
Under the NAIC's[Managing General Agents Act](https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/model-law-225.pdf) , "the acts of the MGA are considered to be the acts of the insurer on whose behalf it is acting," and an MGA "may be examined as if it were the insurer." A compliance check your software missed is not a software problem, but instead it is your carrier's exam finding, and eventually your binding authority.


So when a vendor says its compliance review is 99% accurate, the useful response is a question: accurate at what, measured how, and on whose documents?


This is how to answer that yourself, before signing. For a shortlist of platforms worth testing, see our guide to[AI underwriting compliance software](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/ai-compliance-review-underwriting) . It is the companion to[measuring underwriting summary accuracy](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/underwriting-summary-accuracy-evaluation) — that page asks whether a system read the document correctly, while this one asks whether it caught what was wrong.


## **Key takeaways**


- **One accuracy number is unfalsifiable by construction.** Google's Document AI declines to report accuracy, calling the metric "less meaningful" for documents and substituting F1. Most insurance vendors report exactly that metric, undefined.
- **Measure the missed-violation rate, not accuracy.** If 3% of your policies contain a violation, a system that flags nothing scores 97%. You can absorb false positives; you cannot absorb false negatives.
- **Your pilot is sized by violations, not policies.** A 500-policy set at 3% contains 15 of them — too few to tell 90% recall from 98%, because the confidence intervals overlap.
- **Eight points of recall is roughly 33 missed violations a year** for an MGA writing $150 million in premium. That is the number the pilot exists to estimate.
- **Regulators already publish an error threshold:** 7% for claims practices, 10% for other trade practices, above which errors are "presumed to indicate a general business practice contrary to these laws."


## **Why the published numbers can't be checked**


[Hyperscience states](https://www.hyperscience.ai/platform/) that "customers regularly achieve 99.5% accuracy and 98% automation in their document processing workflows".[Convr advertises](https://convr.com/) "91% machine read data accuracy" for a named customer. But in neither cases, it is specified what counts as correct, at what granularity, on how many documents, or who decided the right answer.


Two vendors break the pattern, in opposite directions. Google[declines to publish an accuracy figure](https://cloud.google.com/document-ai/docs/workbench/evaluate) for Document AI, explaining that the metric "is less meaningful because 1) not all labels appear in the test set... and 2) there may be multiple values for a single label"; it reports precision, recall and F1 instead, computed on your data.


‍[Bevaya](https://labs.bevaya.ai/post/2026-post-train-one-year-later/) , which trades as a dba of Roots Automation, reports results on 346 held-out loss runs with bootstrap confidence intervals — though not the documents themselves, which are client loss runs it cannot release. Its marketing site headlines 98%+ "document extraction accuracy," a field-level figure; on that benchmark, the share of documents with every field correct is 52.9%. Its own engineers explain why the second number is the one that matters: "macro and micro accuracy don't tell you whether any single document is usable."


The standard here is not ours.[NIST's AI Risk Management Framework](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf) says "accuracy measurements should always be paired with clearly defined and realistic test sets – that are representative of conditions of expected use – and details about test methodology." So a percentage with none of that attached is a claim about nothing in particular.


## **What to measure instead**


Compliance review is a detection problem, and its two error types cost wildly different amounts. A **false positive** is a clean policy the system flags: it costs a reviewer a few minutes. A **false negative** is a violation the system passes: it costs you a policy bound outside authority, and it surfaces at a carrier audit or a market conduct exam rather than at your desk. In the[classical definitions](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/evaluation-of-unranked-retrieval-sets-1.html) , precision is the share of flags that are real, recall the share of real violations that were flagged. Recall is the one with teeth, and its complement (the missed-violation rate) is the number to put in the contract.


It also explains why a single accuracy figure actively misleads here. Manning and colleagues put it plainly for skewed data: "A system tuned to maximize accuracy can appear to perform well by simply deeming all documents nonrelevant to all queries."


At a 3% violation rate, flagging nothing scores 97%.


It is worth knowing before the pilot rather than after: at low prevalence, precision collapses even for a good detector.[Positive predictive value](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11569444) is sensitivity × prevalence divided by that plus (1 − specificity) × (1 − prevalence), so at 3% prevalence a system with 85% sensitivity and 94% specificity returns about 30%. Two flags in three will be clean policies — arithmetic, not failure, and[why precision and recall diverge on imbalanced data](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0118432) . Budget reviewer time for it, and don't let a vendor raise precision by tightening thresholds, because that comes straight out of recall.


## **Build the gold set from your own bound policies**


No insurance-specific benchmark for compliance detection exists, and your book is the only test set that predicts your results.


Pull bound policies from the last 12 months, stratified by program, state and carrier — the dimensions your rules vary along. Then record the correct answer for each: every violation present, the rule it breaches, where it sits in the document. Carriers testing extraction from regulatory documents use a similar method; see[regulatory document review at scale](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/regulatory-document-review-carriers) . Two reviewers label independently and a third adjudicates, because a label set one person produced alone is that person's opinion, and accuracy measured against a noisy label is depressed for every vendor alike.


Only then do you seed. Natural violations are too rare to measure against, for reasons the next section makes precise, so construct additional cases by modifying clean policies in ways your compliance team recognises: the endorsement that should have been attached and wasn't, the limit above the program maximum, the state form that was omitted. Record exactly what you seeded. Like[build vs buy underwriting automation](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/build-vs-buy-underwriting-automation-mgas) , the cost of doing this properly is real and smaller than the cost of finding out in production.


## **Size the pilot by violations instead of policies**


This is where most evaluations tend to fail. A 500-policy gold set sounds rigorous, but at a 3% violation rate it contains **15 violations** — and 15 is the number that determines what you can conclude.


Take the two systems concretely. One at 90% recall catches 14 of those 15 and misses one; one at 98% catches all 15. Using the[Wilson score interval](https://repository.upenn.edu/items/ab6bcab6-4515-48a1-82e2-a9311957aa08) — recommended for samples this small, where the textbook Wald interval is unusable — 14 of 15 gives a 95% confidence interval of 70.2% to 98.8%, and 15 of 15 gives 79.6% to 100%. They overlap almost entirely. A 500-policy pilot cannot tell the two apart.


The[sample size for a proportion](https://eurradiolexp.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s41747-024-00474-w) is n = z²·p(1−p)/E², and applied to recall it depends only on the violation count: about **138 violations** to pin recall near 90% to within ±5 points, 35 for ±10. Because sensitivity is estimated only on positive cases, the same source gives n_Sens = z²·Sens(1−Sens)/(E²·P) — so at 3% prevalence, reaching 138 violations by random sampling means pulling roughly **4,600 policies** . That inflation is the whole argument for seeding.


And if a system misses nothing at all, the[rule of three](https://jhanley.biostat.mcgill.ca/c607/ch08/zero_numerator.pdf) says zero events in n observations bounds the true rate at 3/n with 95% confidence. Zero misses across 15 violations bounds the miss rate at 20%; across 138, at 2.2%. A perfect score on a small set is close to no information.


### **What eight points of recall costs**


Convert it to your book.[The Florida Surplus Lines Service Office](https://www.fslso.com/docs/default-source/uploadedfiles/reports/annual-reports-archive/2025-annual-report.pdf) reported an average 2025 premium of $10,831 per commercial general liability policy in Florida's surplus lines market, so an MGA writing $150 million of comparable business binds roughly 13,800 policies a year — about 415 violations passing through annually at a 3% rate.


At 90% recall, 42 reach a bound policy uncaught. At 98%, eight do. The difference between two vendors whose decks both round to "99% accurate" is **roughly 33 missed violations a year** — and the 500-policy pilot could not have told them apart.


Is 3% realistic? It is conservative.[A 2025 Texas market conduct exam](https://tdi.texas.gov/commissioner/disciplinary-orders/documents/20259264.pdf) of a carrier using an MGA found that in 35% of policies reviewed, agents on the declarations page were not appointed to issue or service them. The carrier paid $150,000, in part for failing to perform its required 2022 annual audit of that MGA.


## **Score the pilot**


Run every system on identical inputs, keeping part of the gold set sealed so nothing is tuned to it. Report, per program and per violation type:


- **Recall, with its Wilson interval.** A point estimate alone is not a result.
- **The missed violations themselves.** Read every one. Missing hard cases evenly is a performance gap; missing an entire rule type is a coverage gap.
- **Precision, and the flag volume it implies** — in reviewer-hours per thousand policies, not as a percentage.
- **Seeded and natural cases scored separately.** If they diverge sharply, your seeds are unrealistic and the estimate is soft.
- **Whether each flag cites its evidence** — clause and page. An unsourced flag is a second review, not a finished one.


The NAIC's[Market Regulation Handbook](https://secure.in.gov/idoi/files/Market-Regulation-Handbook-17_Vol1.pdf) treats an error rate above 7% for claims practices or 10% for other trade practices as "presumed to indicate a general business practice contrary to these laws" — the standard your output faces whether a person or a model produced it.


## **Questions that separate an evaluation from a demo**


1. **What is your recall on violations, and on how many?** If the answer is an accuracy percentage, ask again.
2. **Who labelled your ground truth, and did two people label independently?**
3. **Show me your five worst misses.** A vendor who cannot has not looked.
4. **What happens to recall when I tighten precision?** There is a trade. A vendor who denies it has not measured it.
5. **Can we run this on our own documents, before contracting?**
6. **What contractually triggers a re-test?** Models change. Tie re-measurement to any model or pipeline change.


## **The scorecard**


Item What to Record


Violations in the gold set Count — this, not the policy count, sizes your study


Natural vs seeded Split, and how seeds were constructed


Stratification Programs, states, carriers represented


Ground truth Who labelled, double-labelled or not, adjudication method


Recall With 95% Wilson interval, per violation type


Missed violations Listed individually, with the rule each breached


Precision And the flag volume in reviewer-hours per 1,000 policies


Seeded vs natural performance Reported separately


Evidence citation Share of flags pointing to the specific clause


Sealed set result Scored once, at the end


Annualised miss estimate Recall applied to your real policy volume


Re-test trigger What contractually forces a re-run


‍


If a vendor cannot fill this in for their own product, that is information too. Copy this and fill one column per vendor, per program.


## **How FurtherAI fits**


Evaluation Studio exists for this loop:[testing AI workflows before production](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/furtherai-eval-studio) by loading a test set built from your own submissions, defining what good looks like, and comparing versions side by side before anything ships.


Two caveats, by this article's own standard. Our launch post describes test sets of "typically 50 or 100", which is good for catching regressions between versions, below the violation counts above for estimating absolute recall. And we published no compliance-detection recall figure. So we are not asking you to take one on faith, but rather to measure ours the way this page describes, on your policies.


## **Frequently asked questions**


#### Where to buy tools that validate commercial insurance compliance automatically for MGAs?


Start from the measurement rather than the market. Any vendor selling automated compliance validation to MGAs should run on your bound policies before you contract, report recall on violations rather than overall accuracy, show its missed cases, and cite the clause behind every flag. Shortlist on those four, then run the pilot above. A vendor unwilling to be measured on your documents is telling you what the measurement would show.


#### What software do MGAs recommend for ensuring compliance review accuracy?


Recommendations are weak evidence here, because most buyers never measured what they bought. No insurance-specific benchmark for compliance detection exists, so peer reference reflects implementation experience rather than detection quality. Ask procedurally instead: what was your gold set, how many violations did it contain, what recall did you observe, what have you missed since go-live. If they cannot answer, the recommendation is about the relationship, not the accuracy.


#### Where to buy compliance software with verified accuracy for MGAs?


"Verified" is doing heavy lifting there, and almost no vendor in this market meets it. Verification requires a defined test set, a stated metric, disclosed labelling and ideally independent review. Across the document-AI vendors surveyed for this article, none published a test set and none cited an independent audit of an accuracy claim. Treat verified accuracy as something you produce during a pilot, not something you buy pre-attached.


#### How many policies does a compliance AI pilot need?


Policies are the wrong unit. Sizing depends on violations: about 138 to estimate recall near 90% within ±5 points, 35 for ±10. At a 3% natural rate that means roughly 4,600 randomly sampled policies — which is why credible pilots seed violations into a smaller sample and score seeded and natural cases separately.
